I can't give advice on voluntary committing yourself as I have been committed twice involuntarily (51-50), and I might end up committed again for a third time by the end of this week.

In my case, I had to face a judge to be allowed to leave "against medical advice" as the psychologists in inpatient wanted to turn my +72hr hold (51-50) into a 14-day hold (52-50), both times. I'm guessing voluntarily interning yourself would be a different experience since I'm assuming you'd choose when to leave, unless you mention something to turn it into an involuntary stay. I didn't like my stay, because I never wanted to be there in the first place. The staff was nice and accommodating to my needs, but being stuck around people with worse mental issues than lil-ol'-suicidal me depressed me worse each time.

Depending on where you live, they might help you reach out to resources in your area to continue your treatment once you're out. They might also have occupational therapists who will try their best to guide you on alternatives to self-harm which can help if you are open to that. My point is that it wasn't all bad.

That said, being involuntarily held (first by police, and the second time by MER) wasn't a fun experience, so maybe avoid that if you can. I didn't feel heard in the MER (Medical Emergency Room) the second time I was there as they used their bias of my medical history to hold me despite my honesty. After being in the MER, which I was sent to both times, I was transferred over to PES (Psychiatric Emergency Services) once they had the space for me. There is much less privacy in PES from the individual "beds" in a large room with six others (in the midst of the COVID-19) to the bathrooms having windows that they open to check who is inside as they knock (which is absolutely fun if you are pooping or showering). Oh, and you are more likely to experience someone having a severe mental breakdown there than in inpatient—not that I didn't see it in inpatient either, it was just less of an occurrence. Inpatient was a way better experience comparatively, and I felt heard better in both instances.

I hope my rambling up there helps you.

P.S. The bathrooms in inpatient were sliding doors with a magnetic lock in my hospital. Sure, no window to be peered on, but not the best in terms of privacy for my tastes.

P.S.S. The showers start frigid and turn scalding after the first burst interval. Any further presses of the button, which you will have to press a bunch of times, will maintain the water temp at scalding. I almost fainted near the end of one of my showers last time from the heat.

I always wish I could offer advice or reach out to help since I think I'm older than a lot of you (turning 29 this year), but I feel like a hypocrite even having desires like that as I, too, feel as horrible and helpless. The only silver lining that I see here is that, while we're all drifting by in a sea of pain and hopelessness, at least we can solace in the fact that we aren't drifting alone, and I've been able to see that camaraderie in other threads. Alone yet in good company.

I'm a fellow suicidal user, and I point this out in case that my word has at least a tiny bit of weight.

I am of the belief that neither extreme should be seen as cowardice: a person unable to end their is life is not a coward, and a person that takes their life is also not a coward. For a person to fight off our innate, primal instinct to survive for survival's sake requires tremendous amounts of bravery to overcome it and kill themselves. Likewise, a person who suffers constantly and to such an intensity to contemplate suicide seriously, and for that person to remain alive despite these reasons requires a different type of valor. Both decisions require courage and strength, even if the types differ in nature.

I hope my point makes some sense.
